title: The Vines of Reckoning: A Connecticut Jungle Opera
premise:
They say that all operas are about a soprano
who wants to sleep with the tenor, but the
baritone won't let her. See, for example, La Traviata,
Rigoletto, or Carmen.

You are composing the libretto for such an opera.

The setting is the wild jungles of Connecticut,
in the not-so-distant future after global warming has
reclaimed the land. The soprano is an intrepid
explorer searching for the lost city of Hartford.
The tenor is a native poet who has been living in
the jungle for years, writing sonnets to the trees and
composing symphonies for the monkeys.

The baritone is a government agent who has been sent
to stop the soprano from finding the lost city. He
has a secret weapon: a giant robot that can sing
Verdi arias in three different languages.

The soprano and the tenor meet in the jungle and
fall in love. They decide to join forces and find
the lost city together. But the baritone is always
one step behind them, and his giant robot is getting
closer and closer.

scenes.title: The Cartographer's Descent
scenes.author: GPT-5.2
scenes.content:
*The curtain rises on a wall of green—impenetrable, primordial. What was once the Merritt Parkway is now a canyon of strangler figs and ceiba trees, their roots cracking through asphalt like slow-motion lightning. Rusted guardrails arc upward, seized by kudzu, forming natural archways. A faded green highway sign, barely legible, reads: HARTFORD — EXIT 27. Below it, a newer sign—hand-painted on bark—reads: TURN BACK. NOTHING LEFT.*

*Morning light filters through the canopy in cathedral shafts. The air hums with cicadas, dripping moisture, and the distant shriek of macaws—species that should not exist this far north, but the climate has rewritten the rules.*

*From stage right, a rope drops from the canopy. Down it slides MIRABEL CROSS (soprano), the cartographer-explorer—wiry, sunburned, fierce. She wears a battered field vest covered in hand-stitched pockets, each containing instruments: a sextant, a barometer, a hand-cranked radio. On her back, a leather map case. Her boots hit the ground and she crouches, listening.*

### MIRABEL (soprano)
*(recitative, breathless, scanning the terrain)*
Twenty-seven days south from the New Haven perimeter.
Fourteen rivers forded. Three bridges collapsed beneath my weight.
The satellite maps show nothing here but green—
the government's favorite color for erasure.

*(She pulls out a hand-drawn map, comparing it to the terrain.)*
But the old maps don't lie.
The Connecticut River still bends here,
still carries the memory of a city in its current.

*(aria, determined, ascending)*
I am the cartographer of forbidden places,
the woman who draws what power denies.
Every blank space on every sanctioned map
is a confession—
a government admitting what it fears.

Hartford, I have followed your ghost
through swamp and canopy,
through checkpoints and lies,
through nights when the only light
was the phosphor of my own stubborn belief.

They erased you from the records.
I will draw you back into existence.

*She kneels, pressing her palm to the cracked asphalt. She closes her eyes. The jungle noise dims—and beneath it, almost imagined, comes a low pulse: the heartbeat of buried infrastructure, of water still flowing through pipes no one maintains.*

*From the canopy above, a shower of crumpled paper falls—not leaves, but pages. Handwritten sonnets on bark-paper, waterlogged and beautiful. MIRABEL catches one, reads it with growing astonishment.*

### MIRABEL
*(reading aloud)*
"O Hartford, your insurance towers dream
beneath the figs, your actuarial tables
have become the jungle's inventory—"

*(She looks up.)*
Who writes poetry to a dead city?

*A figure drops silently from a branch above—SYLVAN OAKES (tenor), the jungle poet. He is barefoot, lean as a vine, dressed in layers of salvaged fabric dyed green and brown with plant pigments. His hair is long, braided with small feathers. He carries a bamboo writing case and a hand-carved wooden flute. He lands with the ease of someone who has lived among branches for years.*

### SYLVAN (tenor)
*(recitative, guarded but curious)*
I write poetry to a living city.
The dead don't need sonnets.
But a city buried alive—
that needs every word I can give it.

### MIRABEL
You're the poet. The one the smugglers mentioned.
"Mad Oakes," they called you.
"Talks to buildings. Serenades the ruins."

### SYLVAN
*(wry, wounded)*
I prefer "composer-in-residence
of the Connecticut Reclamation Zone."
The monkeys are my orchestra.
The trees are my concert hall.
The audience is... usually just me.

*(He takes back the fallen sonnet, tenderly.)*
Until today.

### MIRABEL
I'm not here for poetry. I'm here for Hartford.

### SYLVAN
*(aria, lyrical, earnest)*
Then you are here for poetry.
Because Hartford is a poem now—
not a place you find on any grid,
but a rhythm you must learn to hear.

I have walked its drowned avenues
by moonlight, knee-deep in warm water,
and I have heard the buildings hum—
not with electricity, but with remembrance.

The old Travelers Tower still stands,
leaning like an ancient singer
who refuses to leave the stage.
At dawn, the vines that grip its sides
vibrate in the wind like strings.

*(He plays a brief, haunting phrase on his flute—the "Hartford motif.")*

That is Hartford's voice.
I didn't compose it.
I only learned to listen.

### MIRABEL
*(moved despite herself)*
You know the way.

### SYLVAN
I know many ways.
But the jungle changes its mind daily.
Paths that existed yesterday are swallowed by morning.
You need someone who speaks the green language.

### MIRABEL
And you need someone with maps.

### SYLVAN
*(studying her, a half-smile forming)*
I need someone who believes
a city can be resurrected with ink.

*A charged silence. They regard each other—two people who have chosen impossible missions, recognizing a kindred stubbornness.*

### MIRABEL & SYLVAN (duet, tentative, then building)
MIRABEL:
I draw lines through chaos—

SYLVAN:
I hear music in the wreckage—

BOTH:
And somewhere in the green cathedral,
a city waits for witnesses.

*Their voices blend for the first time. The jungle responds—birdsong shifting key, monkeys chattering in something almost like approval.*

*But the moment is shattered. From far off, a sound unlike anything natural: a deep, resonant, mechanized voice singing the opening of Verdi's "La donna e mobile"—in Italian, perfect, terrifying.*

### THE COLOSSUS (offstage, mechanized bass)
*(singing, distant but approaching)*
"La donna e mobile
qual piuma al vento..."

*The jungle goes silent. Even the cicadas stop.*

### SYLVAN
*(grabbing MIRABEL's arm, whispering)*
Run.
That is not a bird.
That is not a storm.
That is the government's throat.

### MIRABEL
What is it?

### SYLVAN
They call it the Colossus.
A walking opera house with fists.
It sings Verdi while it searches.
And behind it—

*A crackling amplified voice cuts through the jungle—urbane, menacing, delivered with the precision of a legal brief.*

### COMMANDANT VOSS (baritone, offstage, amplified)
Attention, unauthorized personnel.
You are in violation of Federal Reclamation Statute 47-B.
The territory designated "Former Hartford Metropolitan Area"
is classified, sealed, and forbidden.

*(A pause, almost genteel.)*

Miss Cross. I have read your grant applications.
Fascinating fiction.
Please surrender your instruments and maps.
The Colossus will escort you to processing.

*The mechanical singing resumes—now in French:*

### THE COLOSSUS (offstage)
"La femme est volage
comme plume au vent..."

*Trees sway in the wake of something massive moving through the undergrowth. A metallic glint flashes between the trunks.*

### MIRABEL
*(defiant)*
Processing.
That's what they call it when they erase you.

### SYLVAN
We go deeper.
The jungle is my ally. The Colossus is heavy.
Vines will slow it. Water will confuse it.
But we must move now.

*(He extends his hand to her.)*
Do you trust a mad poet?

### MIRABEL
*(taking his hand)*
I trust anyone the government wants silenced.

*They plunge into the undergrowth together, vanishing into the green. Behind them, the Colossus's Verdi swells—now in English:*

### THE COLOSSUS (offstage, growing louder)
"Woman is fickle
as a feather in the wind..."

### CHORUS OF MONKEYS AND JUNGLE BIRDS
*(erupting from the canopy, chaotic, defiant)*
Run, run, through root and river!
The iron throat is coming!
But the jungle has ten thousand doors
and the government has only one key!

*The stage darkens except for the fading glow of fireflies and the cold, sweeping beam of the Colossus's searchlight, probing the canopy like a mechanical eye.*

*Blackout.*

scenes.title: The Poet's Garden and the Iron Aria
scenes.author: Claude Opus 4.5
scenes.content:
*The curtain rises on a hidden clearing deep in the jungle—SYLVAN's sanctuary. It is a place of astonishing beauty and mad invention. He has cultivated a garden in the ruins of a collapsed shopping mall, its skylights shattered and open to the canopy above. Vines have been trained into archways. Salvaged mirrors redirect sunlight into warm pools where orchids bloom in impossible profusion. Along the walls, hundreds of bark-paper sonnets are pinned, fluttering like moth wings in the humid breeze.*

*Center stage: a grand piano—half-consumed by a fig tree, its keys yellowed but still functional where the roots have not yet reached. The tree's trunk grows through the instrument's body, and when the wind moves through the leaves, the piano's strings murmur sympathetically, producing ghost chords.*

*SYLVAN leads MIRABEL into this space. She stops, stunned. Her cartographer's mind is overwhelmed by a place that resists mapping—a space that is simultaneously ruin, garden, library, and concert hall.*

### MIRABEL (soprano)
*(breathless)*
This is impossible.
A garden in a shopping mall.
A piano married to a tree.
You've built a world inside the wreckage.

### SYLVAN (tenor)
*(modest, lighting salvaged candles)*
Not built. Negotiated.
The jungle wanted to reclaim this space.
I wanted to keep it.
We compromised.

*(He gestures to where vines and human craftsmanship interweave.)*
The fig tree gets the bass notes.
I get the treble.
We share the middle register
and argue about tempo.

*MIRABEL laughs—perhaps for the first time in weeks. She sets down her map case and moves through the garden, touching sonnets pinned to the walls, reading fragments.*

### MIRABEL
*(reading)*
"To the Aetna Diner, whose neon ghost still flickers
in the dreams of every short-order philosopher..."

*(another)*
"Ode to the Bushnell, whose stage now hosts
a company of tree frogs performing Ionesco..."

*(She turns to him.)*
You've written love letters to every building in Hartford.

### SYLVAN
Every building I could find.
Some are underwater. Some are underground.
Some exist only in the memory of their foundations.

*(aria, intimate, confessional)*
I was a poet in the old world too—
but in the old world, poetry was decorative.
A thing you put on shelves
between the bookends of a comfortable life.

Here, poetry is structural.
It holds things up.
My sonnets are the scaffolding
that keeps Hartford from forgetting itself.

Every morning I wake and recite
the names of streets:
Asylum Avenue, Capitol Avenue, Farmington—
because if I stop saying them,
the jungle will swallow the syllables
and the streets will truly die.

*(He sits at the piano, playing around the fig tree's intrusion—a melody that is part composed, part improvised around the notes the tree has claimed.)*

I did not choose solitude.
Solitude chose me
when the world decided
that remembering was treason.

### MIRABEL
*(sitting beside him on the piano bench)*
Then we are both traitors.

*(She pulls out her hand-drawn maps and spreads them across the piano's closed lid.)*

Look—I've mapped the river's new course,
the flood lines, the subsidence zones.
Here—

*(She points.)*
—is where the old capitol should be.
And here—

*(She traces a line.)*
—is a thermal signature I detected from the ridge.
Something is still generating heat underground.
Power systems. Infrastructure.
Hartford isn't just ruins, Sylvan.
Something down there is still running.

### SYLVAN
*(leaning close to study the map, their shoulders touching)*
I've heard it.
At night, when the jungle is quietest,
there's a hum beneath the ground.
I thought it was the earth dreaming.

### MIRABEL
It's generators. Or water treatment. Or both.
Someone designed Hartford to survive.

*Their faces are close now. The candles flicker. The piano tree murmurs a chord that sounds almost deliberate—a musical nudge.*

### SYLVAN
*(softly)*
You know, the monkeys have been watching you
since you arrived.
They do this thing—
when they approve of a newcomer,
they drop fruit on their head.

*A mango drops from above, landing squarely on MIRABEL's map case. They both stare at it, then at each other, then laugh.*

### CHORUS OF MONKEYS (in the canopy above)
*(chattering, musical, approving)*
She reads the land with ink!
He reads the land with song!
Two voices, one direction—
the jungle says: belong!

### MIRABEL & SYLVAN (duet, tender, the love theme)
MIRABEL:
I have mapped coastlines and craters,
drawn borders through disputed lands,
but I never mapped the distance
between two reaching hands.

SYLVAN:
I have written odes to rivers,
sonnets to the patient stone,
but I never found the stanza
that could make a heart feel known.

BOTH:
Here in the green confusion,
where the compass spins and spins,
perhaps the truest map is drawn
where one breath ends
and another begins.

*They almost kiss. The piano tree plays a resolving chord—*

*—which is obliterated by a massive, ground-shaking footfall. Then another. Then a third. The candles gutter. Mirrors rattle on their hooks. Sonnets tear free from the walls and swirl in a sudden wind.*

*The COLOSSUS has found them.*

*It enters upstage, crashing through the mall's remaining wall. It is fully visible for the first time: twelve feet tall, burnished bronze and steel, its chest bearing the faded seal of the Department of Reclamation. Its face is a smooth oval with two searchlight eyes. Its mouth is a grille through which sound pours with operatic force. Its limbs move with hydraulic grace, each step deliberate, each gesture programmed with the vocabulary of a conductor.*

*Riding on its shoulder—literally seated in a custom saddle on the machine's left pauldron—is COMMANDANT VOSS (baritone). He is immaculate: dark uniform, polished boots, thin gloves, a face that has never been surprised. He holds a tablet displaying MIRABEL's file and a small control unit for the Colossus.*

### COMMANDANT VOSS (baritone)
*(recitative, descending from the Colossus with practiced ease)*
Sylvan Oakes.
Poet. Deserter. Unlicensed cultural preservationist.
Your file is thicker than your collected works.

*(He picks up a fallen sonnet, reads it with mock appreciation.)*
"Ode to the Bushnell..."
Charming.
Seditious, but charming.

*(to MIRABEL)*
And you, Miss Cross.
The cartographer who draws maps
to places that officially do not exist.
Do you know what we call that in my department?

### MIRABEL
Courage?

### VOSS
Fraud.

*(He circles them, his boots crisp on the debris-strewn floor.)*

You mistake nostalgia for heroism.
Hartford was decommissioned.
Not destroyed—decommissioned.
Like a ship. Like a satellite.
Its purpose ended.
The state moved on.
The citizens were relocated.
The records were archived—properly, I might add.

### SYLVAN
Archived means hidden.
Relocated means scattered.
Decommissioned means you killed a city
and called it paperwork.

### VOSS
*(aria, smooth, seductive; the bureaucrat's creed)*
I am not the villain of your little story.
I am the man who keeps the world from chaos.
Every border I enforce is a sentence in a grammar
that keeps civilization legible.

You think a city is its buildings?
A city is its function.
And when function ceases,
sentiment is just expensive rot.

I have dismantled fourteen former municipalities.
I have overseen the orderly erasure
of places that no longer served the state.
And I have done it all
without raising my voice.

*(He gestures to the Colossus.)*
The machine raises its voice for me.

### VOSS
Demonstrate, please.

*The COLOSSUS steps forward. Its chest cavity opens slightly, revealing resonating chambers designed like a pipe organ. It draws a mechanical breath—pistons hissing—and begins to sing. The aria is from Verdi's "Il Trovatore"—"Di quella pira"—performed with inhuman precision, first in Italian, then seamlessly shifting to French, then to German.*

### THE COLOSSUS (mechanized bass)
*(aria, thunderous, technically flawless)*
"Di quella pira l'orrendo foco
tutte le fibre m'arse, avvampo!"

"De ce bucher l'horrible flamme
a brule toutes mes fibres, je brule!"

"Von jenem Scheiterhaufen grausig Feuer
hat all mein Innerstes entflammt!"

*The sound is devastating. Glass shatters. Water ripples. The piano tree groans. MIRABEL and SYLVAN are driven to their knees by the sheer volume—not pain, but the overwhelming force of art weaponized.*

### VOSS
*(over the fading echoes)*
Three languages.
Perfect pitch.
No emotion whatsoever.
That is the future of culture, Miss Cross.
Art that serves. Art that obeys.
Art with an off switch.

### MIRABEL
*(rising, ears ringing, furious)*
Art with an off switch isn't art.
It's furniture.

### SYLVAN
*(also rising, moving protectively toward MIRABEL)*
You've built a singer that doesn't know what it's singing.
You've given it Verdi's fire
without Verdi's heart.

### VOSS
Hearts are inefficient.

*(He presses a button on his control unit.)*
Colossus: secure the subjects.
Confiscate all documents, instruments, and maps.
Prepare for extraction.

*The COLOSSUS advances, its arms extending. SYLVAN steps in front of MIRABEL.*

### SYLVAN (tenor)
*(to MIRABEL, urgently)*
The river.
Through the east passage—
the old service corridor beneath the food court.
It leads to the Connecticut River's new channel.
The machine cannot follow through water.

### MIRABEL
Your garden—your sonnets—

### SYLVAN
*(torn, looking at his life's work pinned to the crumbling walls)*
A poet who saves his poems
but loses his reader
has saved nothing.

*(He grabs her hand.)*
Run with me.

*SYLVAN blows a piercing note on his flute—the same "Hartford motif" from Scene 1. The monkeys erupt. Mirrors tilt, flashing blinding light into the Colossus's searchlight eyes. The machine staggers, recalibrating. VOSS shouts orders.*

### VOSS
Override! Compensate! They're—

*But MIRABEL and SYLVAN are already gone, plunging through a gap in the floor into darkness below. The sound of rushing water rises.*

*The COLOSSUS, recovering, begins to follow—but its massive foot crashes through the weakened floor. It is stuck, one leg swallowed by the collapsed sublevel, its Verdi aria stuttering as its systems compensate.*

### THE COLOSSUS
*(glitching, fragments of three languages jumbled)*
"Di quella—femme—Scheiterhaufen—"

### VOSS
*(cold, staring after them into the dark)*
The river.
Of course.

*(He speaks into a communicator.)*
Deploy the acoustic net along the Connecticut.
They'll surface.
They always surface.

*(aria reprise, quiet, menacing)*
I am patient.
I am thorough.
I have erased fourteen cities
and I will erase a fifteenth
if that is what order requires.

But first—
I will erase two dreamers
who believe that love
is louder than law.

*The Colossus finally wrenches itself free, showering debris. Sonnets flutter in the settling dust like wounded birds. VOSS mounts the machine's shoulder once more. It turns, crashing back through the wall it entered, each footstep shaking the stage.*

*In the silence that follows, a single sonnet—pinned higher than the rest, beyond reach—flutters in the breeze. The piano tree, disturbed by the violence, plays one last ghost chord: the Hartford motif, sustaining, refusing to fade.*

### CHORUS OF MONKEYS AND JUNGLE BIRDS
*(soft, mournful, then gathering resolve)*
The garden breaks, the mirrors fall,
the poet's pages scatter.
But ink soaks into living wood—
and living wood remembers.

Run, lovers, to the river's mouth.
The water knows the way.
What iron forgets and power drowns,
the current keeps in play.

*Blackout.*

scenes.title: Hartford Resurgent (Finale: The City That Refused to Die)
scenes.author: GPT-5.2
scenes.content:
*The curtain rises on the true heart of lost Hartford. A vast underground chamber—the old Park River tunnel system, expanded by decades of water and root into something between a cathedral and a cavern. The Connecticut River has carved a new subterranean channel here, flowing through what was once the city's buried waterway, now widened into a glowing underground lake.*

*The space is illuminated by bioluminescent algae coating the walls in rippling blue-green light. Above, root systems from the jungle penetrate the ceiling like chandeliers, some bearing flowers that have never seen the sun. The foundations of Hartford's buildings are visible in cross-section—layers of brick, marble, and steel, like geological strata of human ambition. Embedded in one wall: the cornerstone of the old State Capitol, its date still legible: 1878.*

*Most astonishing: the infrastructure is alive. Water pipes still carry flow. Ancient emergency lights—powered by a geothermal tap the original engineers built as a failsafe—glow amber along walkways. Hartford did not die. It retreated underground and kept breathing.*

*MIRABEL and SYLVAN emerge from a side passage, soaked, gasping, but radiant with discovery. They stand at the edge of the underground lake, staring.*

### MIRABEL (soprano)
*(whispered, then swelling with emotion)*
Sylvan.
Look.

The thermal signature I detected—
this is what's still running.
Hartford built itself a heartbeat
and buried it where no one would think to listen.

### SYLVAN (tenor)
*(touching the glowing walls)*
All those years I walked above,
writing sonnets to what I thought were bones—
and beneath my feet,
the city was alive.

Not a memory.
Not a ghost.
A seed.

*(aria, awestruck, revelatory)*
I wrote you elegies, Hartford,
when I should have written you lullabies.
I mourned you in minor keys
when you were only sleeping.

Forgive a poet his pessimism—
we are trained to love the beautiful wreck,
to find meaning in the falling.
But you—
you refused to fall.

You traded sky for stone,
sunlight for this strange blue glow,
and you kept your pulse
beneath a world that declared you dead.

You are the stubbornest city
I have ever loved.

### MIRABEL
*(kneeling by the water, testing it, recording readings)*
The water is clean.
Filtered through limestone and root systems.
The geothermal tap is maintaining temperature.
Sylvan—people could live here.
This isn't a ruin. This is an ark.

### SYLVAN
*(joining her)*
An ark waiting for passengers.

*They share a look—the weight of what they've found settling on them. This changes everything.*

*A thunderous impact from above. Dust rains down. Then another impact. The COLOSSUS is directly overhead, its footsteps transmitted through the earth like a seismic heartbeat. The bioluminescent algae flickers with each strike, as if the underground city itself flinches.*

*A section of the ceiling cracks. Through it descends a rappelling line, and down it slides COMMANDANT VOSS, immaculate as ever, his boots finding the ground with barely a sound. He surveys the underground chamber with the expression of a man who has just discovered a much larger problem than he anticipated.*

### VOSS (baritone)
*(recitative, genuine surprise breaking through his composure for the first time)*
Well.
This is... unexpected.

*(He touches a glowing wall, pulls his hand back.)*
Infrastructure.
Functioning infrastructure.
This was not in the decommission report.

*(His expression hardens.)*
Which means the original engineers
built Hartford to survive its own erasure.
Clever. Insubordinate. But clever.

*(to MIRABEL and SYLVAN)*
Do you understand what this means?
If this becomes public—
if people learn that a decommissioned city
refused to die—
every sealed zone in the country becomes suspect.
Every erasure becomes questionable.
The entire Reclamation Program unravels.

### MIRABEL
Good.

### VOSS
*(aria, conflicted—for the first time, the bureaucrat confronts the cost of his work)*
I have given my career to order.
I have believed—truly believed—
that civilization requires pruning,
that some branches must be cut
so the trunk survives.

Fourteen cities.
I told myself: necessary.
I told myself: progress.
I told myself: the people were relocated,
the culture was archived,
nothing of value was lost.

*(He looks at the walls, the roots, the flowing water.)*

But you can't archive a river.
You can't relocate a foundation.
And you cannot—

*(His voice breaks, almost imperceptibly.)*

—you cannot decommission
the stubbornness of stone.

### SYLVAN
*(stepping toward VOSS, not with anger but with recognition)*
You hear it too.
The hum.
The city speaking.

### VOSS
*(stiffening)*
I hear plumbing.

### SYLVAN
You hear plumbing that chose to keep flowing
when every order said stop.
That's not infrastructure, Commandant.
That's defiance.

*From above, the COLOSSUS's footsteps halt. A mechanical groan. Then, transmitted through the cracked ceiling, its voice—beginning another Verdi aria, "Va, pensiero" from Nabucco, the chorus of the Hebrew slaves. But something is different. The acoustics of the underground chamber transform the sound. The algae-coated walls resonate. The water amplifies. The mechanical perfection acquires, for the first time, an echo that sounds almost like longing.*

### THE COLOSSUS (from above, transmitted through stone)
*(singing, the aria arriving transformed)*
"Va, pensiero, sull'ali dorate..."
"Go, thought, on golden wings..."

*The three humans freeze, listening. The aria—meant as a weapon, as a tool of control—has become something else entirely, filtered through Hartford's living stone. It sounds like a lament. It sounds like a prayer.*

### MIRABEL
*(to VOSS)*
Do you hear that?
Your machine is singing a song about exile
in a city that was exiled.
And the city is singing back.

*It is true. The underground chamber has begun to resonate—not just with the Colossus's voice, but with its own frequencies. Water moving through pipes creates bass harmonics. The geothermal system hums a drone. Roots vibrate like cello strings. Hartford is accompanying the machine that was sent to enforce its silence.*

### VOSS
*(shaken, reaching for his communicator)*
Colossus—cease.
Cease singing.
That is an order.

*But the Colossus does not stop. The aria continues, growing richer as the city joins in. VOSS presses buttons frantically. Nothing responds. The machine has passed beyond command—not through malfunction, but through resonance. It has found a duet partner older and more persistent than its programming.*

### VOSS
The controls—
they're not responding.
It's the vibrations. The frequencies are interfering with—

### SYLVAN
With orders.
But not with music.

*SYLVAN raises his flute and plays the Hartford motif—the same haunting phrase from Scenes 1 and 2. MIRABEL, seizing the moment, begins to sing. Her voice rises to meet the Colossus's aria, not competing but weaving through it.*

### MIRABEL (soprano)
*(singing with and through the Colossus's "Va, pensiero")*
Go, thought—yes, go—
but not on golden wings.
Go on green ones.
Go on roots and river currents.
Go where no decree can follow.

Hartford, I have found you.
Not as I expected—
not in towers and boulevards—
but in the pulse beneath the stone,
in the water's stubborn sentence:
I am still here.
I am still here.

### SYLVAN (tenor)
*(joining, his voice braiding with hers)*
I am still here—
the poet says it to the page,
the city says it to the earth,
the lover says it to the beloved
who was told he did not exist.

*(He takes MIRABEL's hand.)*
We are all still here.

*VOSS stands apart, his control device useless in his hand. The Colossus above has shifted from "Va, pensiero" to something new—fragments of its three-language Verdi repertoire, but rearranged, recombined, as if the machine is composing for the first time. Italian, French, and German phrases tumble together, no longer precise recitation but genuine, stumbling expression.*

### THE COLOSSUS (from above, voice changing)
*(no longer performing—searching)*
"Pensiero... pensee... Gedanke..."
"Thought... thought... thought..."

*(A pause in the mechanical voice. When it resumes, it is quieter, almost tentative.)*

"Where... is the city?"
"Dove... la citta?"
"I can hear... something beneath me."
"Something... that sings back."

*A massive crack spreads across the ceiling. Not destruction—revelation. Through it, moonlight and jungle starlight pour down, meeting the bioluminescent glow from below. The underground city is no longer underground. The barrier between Hartford's burial and Hartford's resurrection fractures.*

*The COLOSSUS peers down through the crack. Its searchlight eyes dim to something softer. For the first time, it sees the city it was sent to keep hidden. Its chassis trembles—not from malfunction, but from something its engineers never anticipated: recognition.*

### THE COLOSSUS
*(simple, awed, in plain English)*
Beautiful.

### VOSS
*(final recitative, the walls of his conviction crumbling)*
I was told this place was dead.
I was told I was burying nothing.
I was told—

*(He stops. He looks at the cornerstone: 1878. He looks at the flowing water. He looks at MIRABEL and SYLVAN, holding hands in the blue-green light.)*

I was told lies.
And I enforced them.

*(He sets down his control device. He sets down his communicator. He removes his gloves, finger by finger, with the care of a man undressing a former self.)*

Fourteen cities.
I wonder... how many of them
are still breathing underground.

### MIRABEL
*(extending her hand to VOSS)*
Help us find out.

*VOSS stares at her hand. A long moment. The Colossus hums softly above—"Va, pensiero" reduced to its simplest melody, a lullaby version of a slave's lament, sung by a machine discovering mercy.*

*VOSS takes MIRABEL's hand. Not as captor to captive. As citizen to citizen.*

### VOSS (baritone)
*(quietly)*
My name is Adrian.
I haven't used my first name in eleven years.

### SYLVAN
Welcome to Hartford, Adrian.
Population: three.
And one very large soprano.

*He gestures upward to the Colossus. Even VOSS almost smiles.*

*The final ensemble begins. MIRABEL, SYLVAN, and VOSS sing together—three voices that were enemies an hour ago, united by the undeniable evidence of a city that refused to die. Above them, the Colossus provides a bass continuo, its Verdi fragments now woven into the new composition rather than imposed upon it. The monkeys and jungle birds, gathered at the edges of the crack in the ceiling, add their wild descant.*

### MIRABEL, SYLVAN & VOSS (trio, then full ensemble)
MIRABEL:
Let the maps be redrawn—
not by governments, but by rivers.
Let the borders be rewritten
by the roots that refuse to respect them.

SYLVAN:
Let the poems be planted—
not in books, but in living walls.
Let the sonnets grow like orchids
in the cracks of every fallen hall.

VOSS:
Let the orders be rescinded—
not by force, but by evidence.
Let the truth be louder
than the silence I enforced.

ALL THREE:
Hartford lives.
Not as it was—
but as it chose to become.
A city of root and water,
of memory and refusal,
of stubborn, impossible,
unerasable song.

### CHORUS OF MONKEYS AND JUNGLE BIRDS
The lost city is found!
Not by sword, not by crown,
but by a cartographer's hand,
a poet's sound,
and a soldier who learned
to lay his orders down!

### THE COLOSSUS
*(final phrase, all three languages unified into one declaration)*
"Liberta... Liberte... Freiheit..."
"Freedom."

*The bioluminescent light intensifies, filling the underground chamber until it blazes like dawn. The crack in the ceiling widens, and through it the jungle pours—not as invasion but as embrace. Vines lower like ropes. Flowers bloom in fast motion along the ancient walls. Hartford's two worlds—the surface jungle and the underground city—merge into a single, living whole.*

*MIRABEL and SYLVAN embrace center stage, their love no longer a secret kept from the world but a vow made in the light. VOSS stands beside them—not apart, not behind, but alongside, his hands empty and open.*

*The Colossus, still peering down through the widening crack, begins to lower itself—carefully, gently, its massive frame descending into the underground chamber with the delicacy of a dancer. It kneels. The first machine to kneel in Hartford since the factories closed. Its searchlight eyes find the 1878 cornerstone and hold there, as if reading a birthdate.*

*The water rises slightly, catching the moonlight and the bioluminescence, until the entire stage shimmers. The jungle's choir—monkeys, birds, frogs, insects—builds to a crescendo that is not noise but harmony: the sound of a world that has learned to sing together.*

*MIRABEL lifts her hand-drawn map of Hartford—complete now, surface and underground united—and holds it up to the light. The audience can see it: a city reborn, drawn in ink and love and stubborn refusal to forget.*

### MIRABEL (soprano, final line)
Hartford.
I found you.

### SYLVAN (tenor, final line)
No.
Hartford found us.

*The lights blaze to full. The entire company—human, animal, mechanical—holds the final chord. Then, slowly, the bioluminescent glow fades to the soft blue-green of a city at rest. The jungle settles. The water stills. The Colossus's eyes dim to a warm amber, like a night-light left on for a child.*

*Curtain.*
